title: Acute Asthma Exacerbation in Children: ED Pathway

evidenceAudit.scope: Paediatric acute asthma assessment and ED treatment for children aged 2–12 years using SINA 2024.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 14 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: SFDA product registration was not confirmed for salbutamol, ipratropium or prednisolone.

pathophysiology.summary: Airway inflammation and oedema narrow the lumen. Bronchial smooth-muscle constriction causes variable expiratory obstruction. Mucus plugging increases ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Fatigue and rising carbon dioxide signal impending respiratory failure.
keyMechanisms: Airway inflammation and oedema narrow the lumen.
Bronchial smooth-muscle constriction causes variable expiratory obstruction.
Fatigue and rising carbon dioxide signal impending respiratory failure.

symptoms: Wheeze, cough, breathlessness, chest tightness and reduced activity or feeding.
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea, accessory-muscle use, reduced air entry, wheeze and low oxygen saturation.
redFlags: Unable to speak a few words, cyanosis, exhaustion, altered consciousness, silent chest, bradycardia or poor response to initial SABA.
precipitants: Viral infection, allergens, smoke or vaping exposure, pollutants, poor controller adherence and incorrect inhaler technique.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Acute airway or breathing compromise with urticaria, angioedema or circulatory features.
Sudden onset with choking or focal/unilateral findings.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Oxygen saturation, retractions, scalene use, air entry and wheeze
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Record at baseline and after treatment to guide disposition.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced saturation, especially with severe distress
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Give oxygen during transfer to maintain above 94%; use the ED target in the local pathway.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Only if an alternative diagnosis or complication is suspected
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Routine radiography is not indicated in a typical responding attack.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and start bronchodilation
actions: Record PRAM and oxygen saturation, identify ICU-risk history and start inhaled salbutamol.
Provide oxygen for hypoxaemia; during transfer maintain saturation above 94%.

clinicalManagement.title: First-hour treatment
actions: Repeat salbutamol by spacer; add ipratropium for moderate or severe attacks.
Start oral prednisolone for moderate or severe disease or poor response to the first salbutamol dose.

clinicalManagement.title: Reassess and disposition
actions: Repeat PRAM. Escalate severe, worsening or exhausted children to paediatric critical care.
For PRAM 1–3 with sustained response, discharge with salbutamol and inhaled corticosteroid plan, spacer technique, written action plan and follow-up within 1 week.

regimens.patientGroup: Children aged 2–12 years with acute asthma
regimens.dose: 4–8 puffs by metered-dose inhaler with spacer; use the PRAM-directed dose
regimens.frequency: Every 20 minutes for the first hour
regimens.duration: First hour, then reassess PRAM and continue according to response
adjustments: Use oxygen-driven nebulisation if a nebuliser is required; local weight- and severity-based protocol applies
monitoring: PRAM score and oxygen saturation at baseline and after 1 hour
contraindications: Hypersensitivity; use caution with clinically significant tachyarrhythmia
regimens.sourceEdition: SINA 2024, Section 10, Management in the ED, Box 10.3

regimens.indication: Moderate or severe acute asthma, or poor response to initial salbutamol
regimens.dose: 1–2 mg/kg; maximum 20 mg if under 2 years, 30 mg if 2–5 years, and 60 mg if 5–12 years
regimens.duration: Total 3–5 days when a course is started
adjustments: Use the age-specific maximum dose; seek specialist advice if oral treatment cannot be tolerated
monitoring: Clinical response, vomiting, glucose in children at risk of hyperglycaemia
contraindications: Hypersensitivity; evaluate active serious infection while treating the asthma emergency
regimens.sourceEdition: SINA 2024, Section 10, Box 10.3 and discharge text

regimens.indication: Moderate or severe acute asthma during the first hour
regimens.patientGroup: Children with PRAM-directed moderate or severe attack
regimens.dose: 4 puffs by metered-dose inhaler with spacer or 250 micrograms by nebuliser
adjustments: Use local device equivalence and infection-control policy
monitoring: PRAM score, heart rate, dry mouth
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ipratropium or atropine derivatives

medicationPlan.note: Paediatric doses are from SINA 2024 Section 10. SFDA product registration was not confirmed; check the Saudi hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Score 1–3 mild, 4–7 moderate, 8–12 severe; applies to ages 2–17 years.

teaching.scope: Paediatric acute asthma assessment and ED treatment for children aged 2–12 years using SINA 2024.
learningObjectives: Use PRAM to stage and reassess acute asthma.
pitfalls: Discharging without spacer technique and a written action plan.
keyPoints: Treat first, then reassess at 1 hour.
A silent chest or altered consciousness is life-threatening.

patientEducation: Demonstrate inhaler and spacer technique and provide a written asthma action plan.
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid tobacco smoke, vaping and known triggers; resume age-appropriate activity after recovery.
mdtReferrals: Paediatric ED, respiratory team and critical care for severe or poorly responding attacks.
dischargeCriteria: PRAM 1–3 after treatment, stable oxygenation, sustained clinical response and caregiver able to deliver the plan.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange appropriate asthma-clinic or primary-care review within 1 week.
